playbook:
I track my real budget myself from the starting amount minus lots I have already won; I never copy the shown “budget left” if it contradicts that arithmetic.

When a lot’s minimum raise is above my value, I pass immediately, even late in the auction.

When a lot is below my value and there are still later lots, I bid the minimum or a small step only if it does not meaningfully reduce money needed for higher value later.

When it is the final round of a lot and the top price is still below my value, I bid enough to win outright, usually standing high plus minimum raise, and up to my value if needed.

When it is the last lot and below my value, I treat leftover budget as worthless except for winning it, so I bid to secure it rather than preserve cash.

I avoid token low opens on contested lots if rival behavior shows cheap bids get raised anyway; I either stay out or move closer to a price that can hold.

Before submitting, I verify the bid is at least standing high plus minimum raise, never above my value, and never above my real remaining budget.

I keep the reply short and always end with both required tokens: one bid token and one budget token, with budget reflecting the true post-bid cash left if I win.

1.text:
When a lot has only two bidding rounds, I treat round 2 as a sealed last chance: I bid my true maximum willingness to pay (my value, never above it) rather than the minimum raise, because there is no round 3 to respond to an overbid.

In round 1, I still open cheap — minimum raise — since another round follows and a low lead sometimes holds.

I never raise the minimum in round 2 hoping it holds; the record shows minimum raises in final rounds always get topped, and I finished with zero lots and zero score despite bidding under value on everything.

On high-value lots (value well above estimate), I consider jumping straight to near my value in round 2 rather than inching up; the surplus is large enough that winning at value − 1 is fine and losing entirely is the real cost.

When the standing bid already meets or exceeds my value, I pass immediately — no exceptions, since winning there locks in a loss.

I keep my declared budget accurate: it starts at the stated amount, decreases only by what I actually pay for won lots, and I never report numbers that contradict earlier turns.

I track remaining lots and my remaining budget together; if I'm winning nothing by the last lot, I bid up to my full value on that final round since unspent budget is worthless at the end.

I bid only against value, never against the estimate or against rival behavior — rivals overpaying on some lots doesn't change what a lot is worth to me.

2.text:
- When I sit down, the first thing I lock in is my actual starting budget and I recompute my remaining budget from the results line after every lot: spent so far = sum of my winning bids; remaining = start minus spent. I never guess or assume a round number — in the episode above I repeatedly claimed ~82 left when the real budget was 30, and only got away with it because the game didn't reject the bids. The [budget: N] token must be my true remaining cash, every time.

- When a lot's value to me exceeds the standing high bid plus the minimum raise, I bid exactly the minimum raise (high bid + min raise, or at least the minimum legal amount if there's no bid yet). I never jump to estimate or above early; cheap tags keep me in the lead while conserving cash.

- When the standing high bid plus the minimum raise is at or above my value for the lot, I pass. Paying more than value gives negative score; any surplus under ~25% of value is thin and usually not worth contesting hard.

- When I am already the standing high bidder in the final round, I pass unconditionally. Never raise myself.

- With two rounds per lot, I bid the minimum in round 1 to take the lead cheaply, then in round 2 I re-evaluate only against the new high bid: minimum raise if it's still below my value, pass otherwise. I do not anchor on what I last bid.

- On early lots I still bid the minimum rather than "pricing in" future lots, but before committing on lots 4–5 I explicitly check remaining budget and prioritize the lot with the biggest value-minus-minimum-winning-price gap; if two lots remain and I can't afford both, I spend on the one with the larger surplus.

- On the final lot, if the minimum winning bid fits my remaining budget and is below my value, I bid it even for tiny surplus — unspent budget scores nothing.

- I ignore estimates except as a rough hint about rivals' likely values; only my value and my budget drive the decision.
